cosy-lesson.title: Since When Is Information Consumption Considered Rest?

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: to introduce the topic and clarify key target vocabulary for the session.

cosy-slide.cosy-instruction: Review the key vocabulary for this session below:

cosy-blockquote.p: Cognitive overload ≠ Restorative rest – excessive mental processing caused by too much input ≠ deep mental recovery that restores energy.

p.em: Example: Swiping through endless short videos causes cognitive overload instead of delivering genuine restorative rest.

cosy-blockquote.p: Information consumption ≠ Mindful stillness – absorbing digital media, news, and notifications ≠ being present without incoming digital distraction.

p.em: Example: Constant information consumption keeps the nervous system active, suppressing peaceful mindful stillness.

cosy-blockquote.p: Pseudo-relaxation ≠ Deep rejuvenation – activities that feel like breaks but actually tire the brain ≠ genuine rest that renews physical and mental vitality.

p.em: Example: Doomscrolling in bed is a form of pseudo-relaxation that prevents true deep rejuvenation during downtime.

cosy-blockquote.p: Digital fatigue ≠ Physical tiredness – exhaustion caused by screen exposure and media processing ≠ bodily fatigue resulting from physical exercise.

p.em: Example: Sitting on the couch scrolling feeds produces digital fatigue rather than the healthy physical tiredness of outdoor exercise.

cosy-blockquote.p: Active leisure ≠ Passive consumption – engaging hobbies that involve physical or creative effort ≠ mindlessly absorbing stream content.

p.em: Example: Gardening and painting represent active leisure, while watching recommended video loops is passive consumption.

cosy-blockquote.p: Sensory deprivation ≠ Constant stimulation – reducing external sights and sounds to calm the mind ≠ continuous input of bright light and audio.

p.em: Example: A walk in a quiet forest provides sensory deprivation, counteracting the constant stimulation of city feeds.

cosy-blockquote.p: Attention fragmentation ≠ Sustained focus – splitting concentration into short bursts across multiple media ≠ focusing deeply on a single task.

p.em: Example: Bite-sized video clips foster attention fragmentation, making sustained focus on long books difficult.

cosy-blockquote.p: Boredom tolerance ≠ Impulse gratification – the capacity to sit comfortably without external entertainment ≠ seeking immediate digital rewards upon feeling bored.

p.em: Example: Developing boredom tolerance is essential for creative thinking, whereas impulse gratification keeps the brain hooked.

cosy-blockquote.p: Mental sanctuary ≠ Algorithmic noise – a peaceful personal space free from external media pressures ≠ automated content streams competing for attention.

p.em: Example: Protecting your bedroom as a mental sanctuary helps shield sleep routines from algorithmic noise.

cosy-blockquote.p: Cognitive recovery ≠ Continuous processing – allowing brain neural pathways to reset without new information ≠ keeping the mind active without pausing.

p.em: Example: True cognitive recovery happens during quiet walks or sleep, not during continuous processing of video streams.

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: pair/group discussion on core session themes.

cosy-slide.cosy-group-instruction: In pairs or small breakout groups, discuss the following questions:

ol.li:
Why do so many people mistake high-volume cognitive overload ≠ restorative rest for a relaxing break after work?
★ Have you ever felt mentally exhausted after spending an hour doing 'nothing' on your phone?

How does constant information consumption ≠ mindful stillness alter our brain's ability to process emotions and daily experiences?
★ When was the last time you sat quietly without listening to a podcast, music, or looking at a screen?

Is doomscrolling a form of pseudo-relaxation ≠ deep rejuvenation that tricks us into feeling relaxed while keeping our nervous system on high alert?
★ What is your favorite non-digital way to unwind after a high-stress day?

What are the long-term health consequences of suffering from digital fatigue ≠ physical tiredness without realizing it?
★ Do you experience eye strain or headaches after spending long evenings on social media apps?

Why has modern society shifted from active leisure ≠ passive consumption toward automated video streams?
★ Do you find it harder to start a creative hobby now than you did a few years ago?

How does giving our brains zero moments of sensory deprivation ≠ constant stimulation affect our sleep quality and dream cycles?
★ Do you check your smartphone right before turning off the lights to sleep?

Is severe attention fragmentation ≠ sustained focus making it nearly impossible for people to enjoy long movies or thick books?
★ How often do you pause a film or show to check messages on your phone?

Why is developing boredom tolerance ≠ impulse gratification crucial for creative problem solving in adult life?
★ What do you do when waiting in a doctor's office or bus stop—reach for your phone or daydream?

How can individuals establish a true mental sanctuary ≠ algorithmic noise in their home environments?
★ Do you have screen-free zones or screen-free times in your daily routine?

Why is uninterrupted cognitive recovery ≠ continuous processing necessary for deep learning and memory consolidation?
★ How do you feel on days when you deliberately leave your phone in another room for several hours?

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: deeper debate and statement evaluation in pairs/groups.

cosy-slide.cosy-group-instruction: In pairs, debate and state whether you agree or disagree with these statements:

ol.li:
Modern technology platforms trick users into treating cognitive overload ≠ restorative rest as relaxation to keep screen time metrics high.
★ Do you feel tech companies deliberately design apps to prevent users from taking real rest breaks?

Replacing quiet reflection with endless information consumption ≠ mindful stillness is destroying our capacity for original thought.
★ Where do your best ideas usually come to you—while scrolling online or while doing quiet chores?

Swiping short-form videos is a form of pseudo-relaxation ≠ deep rejuvenation that actually increases long-term anxiety levels.
★ Have you ever felt anxious after spending hours watching short videos late at night?

Society underestimates the threat of digital fatigue ≠ physical tiredness, treating mental exhaustion as laziness rather than screen overload.
★ Do you think workplaces should offer mandatory screen-free breaks during office hours?

Engaging in active leisure ≠ passive consumption requires more initial discipline, but yields far greater life satisfaction.
★ Is there an active hobby like playing an instrument or crafting that you wish you spent more time on?

Without intentional moments of sensory deprivation ≠ constant stimulation, modern humans will permanently lose the ability to relax naturally.
★ Could you spend a weekend at a quiet cabin with zero internet access without feeling anxious?

The spread of attention fragmentation ≠ sustained focus will force schools and universities to abandon deep reading assignments.
★ Do you find reading printed paper books easier or harder than reading articles on a screen?

Rebuilding boredom tolerance ≠ impulse gratification is the most important mental skill for the next generation.
★ Should parents limit smartphone access for children until they reach high school age?

Establishing a phone-free mental sanctuary ≠ algorithmic noise at home is essential for preserving healthy family relationships.
★ Do you have rules in your home about keeping phones away from the dinner table?

Prioritizing cognitive recovery ≠ continuous processing is a necessary act of personal resistance against the attention economy.
★ What is one boundary you can set today to protect your quiet mind from digital overload?

ul.li: Incorrect: Scroll reels make → Correct: Scrolling reels makes ((Grammar gerund subject: Gerund 'scrolling' requires singular verb agreement 'makes'))
Incorrect: I → Correct: I ((Word order: Transitive verb + direct object + temporal modifier))
Incorrect: We discussed about → Correct: We discussed X ((Extra word deletion: 'discuss' is transitive and does not take preposition 'about'))
